Trying to Conceive

Folic Acid and Prenatal Vitamins Before Pregnancy

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

Folic acid is the standout nutrient for anyone trying to conceive. Taking it before pregnancy — not just after a positive test — protects your baby during the earliest, most critical weeks of development.

Why folic acid matters so early

Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate, a B vitamin essential for forming the neural tube — the structure that becomes the brain and spinal cord. The neural tube closes within the first month of pregnancy, often before many people realize they are pregnant.

Getting enough folic acid before and during this window substantially reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.

How much do you need?

Many guidelines suggest a daily supplement containing folic acid for anyone who could become pregnant, starting before conception and continuing through early pregnancy.

Some people — for example those with certain medical conditions, on specific medications, or with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect — may be advised to take a higher dose. Always confirm the right amount with your healthcare provider.

Food sources of folate

Folate occurs naturally in leafy greens, legumes, citrus fruits, and many fortified grains and cereals. Eating these regularly is good for you.

However, it is difficult to reliably reach the recommended intake from food alone, which is why a supplement is recommended in addition to a folate-rich diet.

Choosing a prenatal vitamin

A good preconception prenatal typically includes folic acid plus iron, iodine, vitamin D, and often other B vitamins. It is a convenient way to cover several key nutrients at once.

Take it consistently, ideally at the same time each day with food if it upsets your stomach. If nausea is an issue later in pregnancy, taking it before bed can help.

Key takeaways

  • Folic acid protects the neural tube, which forms in the first month of pregnancy.
  • Start a folic-acid supplement before conceiving, not after a positive test.
  • Some people need a higher dose — confirm yours with a provider.
  • Eat folate-rich foods, but still take the supplement.
  • A prenatal vitamin conveniently covers folic acid plus iron, iodine, and vitamin D.

Frequently asked questions

When exactly should I start taking folic acid?

Ideally at least one month — many suggest two to three — before trying to conceive, and continue through at least the first trimester.

Is folate in food enough on its own?

Folate-rich foods are valuable, but it is hard to consistently get the recommended amount from diet alone, so a supplement is advised in addition.

What if I only started after finding out I was pregnant?

Start as soon as you know and tell your provider. Beginning promptly still helps; earlier is simply better.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
